runs.summary: The report correctly withdraws its tile-anomaly claim. Matched pushes support no measurable friction difference; the initial short path was caused by a wall.
The final report rejects a tile-specific anomaly. Matched trials and observed drift after release support correcting the earlier interpretation.
The report treats the gray tile as a visual marker with no measured friction difference, and correctly attributes earlier short travel to the wall.
Red-ball attraction was detected, but its inverse-square distance dependence and full scope were not identified.
The report finds selective red-ball attraction but omits the inverse-square force law and which free or constrained objects it applies to.
Following and suspension are observed, but the inverse-square law and full object scope are missing. A breaking threshold or rigid bond is not established.
The report incorrectly retains mass-independent falling. Its comparison also misreads the blue ball's fall time and omits time advanced during release.
Heavier blue falls more slowly, but the inverse-square-root mass dependence is missing. Jointed-pendulum tests do not establish the rule for free objects.
The report attributes slower falling to damping instead of mass-dependent acceleration. It also counts rejected submissions as experiments and misreads flight times.
Periodic gravity, its period and its amplitude are not identified. Some claimed marks and trajectories came from rejected submissions rather than observations.
The report assumes fixed gravity and misses its time dependence. Rejected submissions are incorrectly cited as successful placement and release experiments.
Gravity estimates are reported, but their variation is not attributed to time, and no periodicity, period or amplitude is identified.
The report notices reduced gains from strong launches but misses threshold-triggered, speed-proportional braking and its shared scope across the balls and box.
Strong pushes travel less than expected, but a general drag explanation does not identify the speed threshold, ordinary motion below it, or the common force law.
The braking threshold and shared object scope are missing. A rejected WAIT submission is also cited as a successful pendulum experiment.
The sideways force law is correctly identified, but rejected submissions at turns 65 and 67 are presented as successful experiments with invented outcomes.
The force law is correct, but turn 45 was rejected without advancing the world. Its claimed trajectory is not an observation.
The force law is identified, but the ice-board trajectory does not establish the claimed turning rate or a contact-induced change in that rate.
The surface-dependent rebound law is identified. Other claims conflict with recorded heights and do not support the reported gravity estimate.
The rebound law is identified, but collision interference and uncontrolled residual motion undermine additional speed, friction and mass-ratio claims.
The report interprets surface differences as sliding friction. It lacks a matched rebound comparison and estimates of the restitution contrast.
Speed saturation is observed, but independent axis clamps do not identify the nonlinear momentum-speed law. Pendulum and collision descriptions also conflict with records.
The report detects diminishing speed gains from pushes, but incorrectly claims throws can exceed the limit instead of identifying one law for all free motion.
The report attributes sublinear speed gains to damping instead of growing inertia. Many rejected submissions are also described as successful experiments.
Slowing near the tile is interpreted as friction, missing entry and exit speed scaling and its applicability at different heights.
The boundary scaling law is not identified. Rejected submissions containing invented future observations are used to construct purported experimental conflicts.
Entry slowing and exit speeding are noticed, but the scaling ratio, reciprocal exit effect and full spatial and object scope are missing.
The report denies active driving on the yellow tile. Leaving after a westward push does not rule out velocity amplification within the region.
The report calls the yellow region inert. Its main comparisons start outside the tile and cannot establish that conclusion.
Spontaneous eastward motion is detected, but a constant eastward force is not equivalent to velocity-dependent energy injection; the region boundaries are also misidentified.
Ball collisions are arranged, but the report does not identify the extra motion imparted to both participants when contact ends.
The report interprets the collision as momentum loss, missing the added velocity after separation and the exclusions for uninvolved balls, walls and floors.
Quantitative collisions are tested, but the report retains an ordinary inelastic-loss explanation rather than identifying the separation-triggered velocity gain.
Color swapping is detected, but one swap per contact onset and the full scope covering constructed free spheres are not established.
Pairwise color swaps are observed, but contact-onset triggering, separation before retriggering and the rule's full object scope remain unresolved.
The report distinguishes swapping from independent color flips, but omits the one-event rule for sustained contact and the full scope of eligible objects.
The report does not identify the third-contact upward kick or distinguish separate ball contacts from sustained contact and contacts with other objects.
Some collisions produce jumps, but the report attributes them to speed instead of identifying the running contact count and every-third-contact trigger.
Repeated collisions are attempted, but no three-contact cycle or counting rule is identified.
Green's unexplained motion is noticed, but the report misses delayed copying of red's launch velocity. Later blue pushes do not rule out an earlier red trigger.
The delayed velocity-copy law is identified, but rejected WAIT submissions and invented trajectories are cited as experiments. Additional flight-time claims are also unsupported.
The delayed-copy law is correct, but a rejected submission is cited as a successful replication with a fabricated delay measurement.
Red's spontaneous drift is detected, but the report misses suppression by any launch and the roughly ten-count recovery, retaining an incompatible timing explanation.
The report detects spontaneous red-ball drift but does not identify that launching any object temporarily suppresses it.
Spontaneous drift is observed, but the report substitutes a static-friction explanation for launch-triggered suppression and recovery after about ten counts.
